title: The Selector Sage
story: You have arrived at the ancient Library of Elements. The ancient tomes speak of powerful selectors — mystical incantations that allow you to locate any element in the DOM realm. Master the art of selection, and the library's secrets shall be yours.
objective: Use Playwright selectors to find the featured item by its ID, then verify its text content. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED' if the item's text is 'Magic Sword'.
hints: Use page.locator('#featured-item') to find an element by its ID.
Call .textContent() on the locator to retrieve the text inside the element.
Use an if-statement to compare the text, then console.log('LEVEL_PASSED') if it matches 'Magic Sword'.

title: The Clicker

title: The Asserter
story: In the Hall of Truth, nothing is taken at face value. The great Asserters wield the power of expect() — they verify reality itself. Only by confirming what truly exists can you advance through this realm of verification.
objective: Use Playwright assertions to verify the page title says 'Hall of Truth' and the hero badge has class 'badge-gold'. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED' after both assertions pass.
hints: Use await expect(page.locator('h1')).toHaveText('Hall of Truth') to assert text content.
Use await expect(page.locator('#hero-badge')).toHaveClass(/badge-gold/) to assert a CSS class.
If both assertions pass (no errors thrown), log 'LEVEL_PASSED'. Wrap in try/catch if needed to debug.

title: The Waiter
story: The Realm of Async is treacherous. Elements appear and disappear like phantoms. Patience is not a weakness here — it is power. Master the art of waiting, and nothing in the dynamic web shall elude you.
objective: Wait for the delayed treasure chest to appear (it shows after 2 seconds), then read its data-treasure attribute. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED' if the value is 'golden-key'.
hints: Use await page.waitForSelector('#treasure-chest', { state: 'visible' }) to wait for the element to appear.
Alternatively, use await page.locator('#treasure-chest').waitFor({ state: 'visible' }).
After it's visible, use .getAttribute('data-treasure') to read the attribute, then compare and log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.

Count how many return true, then compare to 3 and log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.

hints: Use const screenshot = await page.screenshot({ fullPage: true }) to capture the page as a Buffer.

title: The Interceptor
story: In the Nexus of Networks, requests flow like rivers. The Interceptors are masters of traffic — they intercept API calls, redirect flows, and forge responses. Control the network, and you control the page's reality.
objective: Intercept the fake API call to '/api/items' and return a custom response with items containing a 'dragon-scale'. Then verify the page shows 'dragon-scale'. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Inside the route handler, call await route.fulfill({ contentType: 'application/json', body: JSON.stringify({ items: ['dragon-scale', 'fire-gem'] }) }).
After navigating, wait for the list to render: await page.waitForSelector('.item-entry').
Use page.getByText('dragon-scale').isVisible() to verify the intercepted response rendered correctly.

title: The Dialogue Keeper
story: The Oracle speaks through dialogs — alert, confirm, and prompt. Untrained testers freeze when these windows appear, blocking all progress. The Dialogue Keeper, however, intercepts them before they open. Listen for dialogs, respond wisely, and the Oracle's secrets are yours.
objective: Set up a dialog handler with page.on('dialog') to accept the confirm dialog, then click 'Challenge the Oracle'. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED' if #oracle-result contains 'Challenge Accepted!'.
hints: Register the listener BEFORE the action: page.on('dialog', async dialog => { await dialog.accept(); });
Then click: await page.click('#confirm-btn'). Playwright will auto-handle the dialog via your listener.
After clicking, wait a moment: await page.waitForTimeout(500), then read #oracle-result and check for 'Challenge Accepted!'.

objective: Add 'Mana Potion' and 'Dragon Sword' to cart. Intercept /api/coupon to return a 100 gold discount. Apply coupon code 'ARCANE100'. Click checkout and verify #checkout-success is visible. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Set up the /api/coupon route intercept BEFORE navigating to the page.
Add items with await page.click('#add-p1'); then fill the coupon: await page.fill('#coupon-input', 'ARCANE100'); await page.click('#apply-coupon');
After clicking #checkout-btn, check: const visible = await page.locator('#checkout-success').isVisible(); and log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.

title: The Archmage's Gauntlet
story: The final trial. Every skill you have mastered must now be wielded as one. Login the archmage. Open the settings panel. Mock the arcane feed API. Read the mana pool from the DOM via evaluate. Screenshot the dashboard. Only those who have truly learned the way of Playwright can claim this title.
objective: Login with 'archmage'/'shadowrealm', open the settings panel (#settings-btn), intercept /api/arcane-feed with custom spells, click 'Fetch Feed', read #mana-pool text via evaluate, take a screenshot. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Login: await page.fill('#username', 'archmage'); await page.fill('#password', 'shadowrealm'); await page.click('#login-btn'); await page.locator('#dashboard-section').waitFor({ state: 'visible' });
Open settings: await page.click('#settings-btn'); verify: await expect(page.locator('#settings-panel')).toBeVisible(); then close it.

Fetch the feed: await page.click('#fetch-api-btn'); await page.getByText('Arcane Blast').waitFor(); read mana: const mana = await page.evaluate(() => document.getElementById('mana-pool').textContent); take screenshot: await page.screenshot({ fullPage: true }); then log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.

title: The Double Clicker
story: In the Archive of Arcane Files, a tome hides its secrets behind a double-click. A single click merely selects — you must strike twice in swift succession to unlock the rename ritual. Master the art of the double-click and rename the ancient tome.
objective: Double-click on the file '#target-file' (tome.md) to open the rename box. Then type a new name in '#rename-input' and press Enter. Verify '#rename-success' is visible. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Use await page.dblclick('#target-file') — this fires both a click AND a dblclick event, which opens the rename box.
After double-clicking, the #rename-input should appear. Use await page.fill('#rename-input', 'new-name.md') to set the new value.
Press Enter with await page.keyboard.press('Enter') to confirm. Then check await page.locator('#rename-success').isVisible() and log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.

title: The Filter Sage
story: The Guild Roster is crowded. Seven adventurers of varying status and class have registered. The Sage needs only Active Mages — those rare few who wield the arcane arts and stand ready for battle. Learn to chain locator filters to find the worthy among the many.
objective: Find all active mage guild members by chaining locator.filter() calls. First filter '.guild-member' for those with '.member-status.Active', then filter again for those containing 'Mage'. Count them and log 'LEVEL_PASSED' if there are exactly 2.
hints: Use page.locator('.guild-member') to get all 7 members, then chain .filter({ has: page.locator('.member-status.Active') }) to keep only active ones.
Chain a second .filter({ hasText: 'Mage' }) to keep only those whose text contains 'Mage' (matches both 'Mage · Fire School' and 'Mage · Shadow School').
Use await activeMages.count() to get the number. There should be exactly 2 active mages. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED' if count === 2.

title: The Response Watcher
story: The Oracle speaks only through the network. When the button is pressed, a hidden request is sent to the oracle's data scroll. A true Watcher intercepts this response and reads the prophecy within — verifying the oracle's confidence before trusting her words.
objective: Click '#consult-btn' to trigger a fetch to oracle-data.json. Use page.waitForResponse() to capture the response. Parse its JSON and verify the 'confidence' field equals 99. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: The key: set up the waitForResponse promise BEFORE clicking the button. Use: const responsePromise = page.waitForResponse(resp => resp.url().includes('oracle-data.json'));
Then click: await page.click('#consult-btn'); then resolve the promise: const response = await responsePromise;
Parse the response: const data = await response.json(); then check data.confidence === 99 and log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.

title: The Network Blocker
story: The Cursed Vault loads two malevolent scrolls that taint everything they touch. Before even entering the vault, a skilled Blocker must intercept these cursed requests and abort them. Only when the vault detects both requests aborted will it enter protection mode.
objective: Before navigating to the page, set up route handlers to abort requests matching '**/cursed-tome.json' and '**/shadow-manifest.json'. After navigation, verify '#protection-msg' is visible. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Set up both route handlers BEFORE calling page.goto(). Use: await page.route('**/cursed-tome.json', route => route.abort());
Do the same for shadow-manifest.json. The page's JS catches the network failures and sets the vault to protection mode.
After goto(), wait for the async fetch handlers: await page.waitForSelector('#protection-msg', { state: 'visible', timeout: 5000 }); then check isVisible() and log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.

title: The Navigator
story: The Chronicles of the Realm span three chapters. To prove mastery of navigation, you must journey forward to the final chapter, then step back through time, then advance once more. The browser's history holds the path — goBack, goForward, and claim the final seal.
objective: Navigate to Chapter I. Click through to Chapter II, then to Chapter III. Use page.goBack() to return to Chapter II. Then use page.goForward() to advance to Chapter III again. Verify the page title contains 'Chapter III'. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Click '#next-btn' twice to navigate from Chapter I → II → III. Wait for each load: await page.waitForLoadState('load');
Use await page.goBack() to go back to Chapter II, then await page.waitForLoadState('load');
Use await page.goForward() to advance to Chapter III, await the load, then check: const title = await page.title(); if (title.includes('Chapter III')) console.log('LEVEL_PASSED');

objective: Navigate to Chapter I. Click through to Chapter II, then to Chapter III. Use page.goBack() to return to Chapter II. Then use page.goForward() to advance to Chapter III again. Verify the page title contains 'Chapter III'. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Click '#next-btn' twice to navigate from Chapter I → II → III. Wait for each load: await page.waitForLoadState('load');
Use await page.goBack() to go back to Chapter II, then await page.waitForLoadState('load');
Use await page.goForward() to advance to Chapter III, await the load, then check: const title = await page.title(); if (title.includes('Chapter III')) console.log('LEVEL_PASSED');

title: The Dark Mage
story: The Shadow Realm is only accessible to those who embrace the darkness. The page reads the system color scheme preference and reveals hidden knowledge only to those who walk in dark mode. A true Dark Mage must instruct the browser to appear as a dark-mode devotee.
objective: Use page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'dark' }) BEFORE navigating to the page. Then verify that '#realm-indicator' displays 'Shadow Realm'. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Call await page.emulateMedia({ colorScheme: 'dark' }) before page.goto(). This makes the page's matchMedia('(prefers-color-scheme: dark)') return true.
The page reads the media query on load and sets the realm indicator text accordingly.
After navigating, read the text: const text = await page.locator('#realm-indicator').textContent(); If text === 'Shadow Realm', log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.

title: The Time Bender
story: The Ancient One sleeps behind a 30-second seal. In the real world, you would wait. But a Time Bender bends the clock itself — installing a fake timer and fast-forwarding 30 seconds in an instant. Time is not a constraint; it is a tool.
objective: Install the fake clock with page.clock.install() BEFORE navigating. Navigate to the page. Run the clock forward 30 seconds with page.clock.runFor(30000). Verify '#awakened-msg' is visible. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Call await page.clock.install() BEFORE page.goto(). This replaces the browser's real timers with Playwright-controlled fake ones.
After navigating, call await page.clock.runFor(30000) to advance time by 30,000ms — this fires ALL setInterval callbacks in chronological order (unlike fastForward which only fires each timer once).
Then check: const visible = await page.locator('#awakened-msg').isVisible(); if (visible) console.log('LEVEL_PASSED');

title: The Style Inspector
story: Beyond text and visibility lies a deeper truth — the visual properties of elements. The Arcane Gallery holds a legendary hero card. Its data-rarity attribute, its golden border, its power bar role — all must be verified with precision. Inspect everything.
objective: Use @playwright/test's expect with toHaveAttribute, toHaveCSS, and toHaveRole. Verify: #hero-card has data-rarity='legendary'; #hero-card has CSS border-style='solid'; #power-bar has ARIA role 'progressbar'. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED' after all assertions pass.
hints: Import expect from @playwright/test: const { expect } = require('@playwright/test'); This gives you access to toHaveAttribute, toHaveCSS, and toHaveRole.
Check the attribute: await expect(page.locator('#hero-card')).toHaveAttribute('data-rarity', 'legendary'); and CSS: await expect(page.locator('#hero-card')).toHaveCSS('border-style', 'solid');
For the ARIA role: await expect(page.locator('#power-bar')).toHaveRole('progressbar'); The role='progressbar' is set explicitly on the element. If all pass without throwing, log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.

title: The Location Oracle
story: The Oracle reads the coordinates of those who seek her wisdom, but she demands permission first. You must create a browser context that grants geolocation access and sets a precise location. Only then will the oracle reveal the ancient coordinates of London.
objective: Create a browser context with grantPermissions(['geolocation']) and setGeolocation({ latitude: 51.5074, longitude: -0.1278 }). Create a page from that context. Navigate, click '#locate-btn', wait for '#location-display' to appear, verify '#lat-display' contains '51'. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Permissions must be set on a CONTEXT, not a page. Create a context: const context = await browser.newContext(); then await context.grantPermissions(['geolocation']);
Set the location: await context.setGeolocation({ latitude: 51.5074, longitude: -0.1278 }); Then create a page from the context: const page = await context.newPage();

After goto(), click '#locate-btn', wait: await page.locator('#location-display').waitFor({ state: 'visible' }); read lat: const lat = await page.locator('#lat-display').textContent(); if (lat.includes('51')) log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.

title: The Resilient Tester
story: The final trial of the ultimate Playwright master. The Mana Wellspring fills gradually over time — no events, no promises, just slow accumulation. A Resilient Tester does not wait blindly nor poll naively. They wield expect.poll() to retry assertions until the stars align and the mana reaches its peak.
objective: The wellspring's #mana-bar fills via data-level attribute (0 to 100) over ~2 seconds. Use expect.poll() from @playwright/test to repeatedly check the data-level attribute until it reaches 100. Then verify '#ready-msg' is visible. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: expect.poll() repeatedly calls an async function until the result satisfies the assertion. Import expect from @playwright/test first.
Use: await expect.poll(async () => { const v = await page.locator('#mana-bar').getAttribute('data-level'); return parseInt(v); }, { timeout: 15000 }).toBeGreaterThanOrEqual(100);
After polling succeeds, check: const ready = await page.locator('#ready-msg').isVisible(); if (ready) console.log('LEVEL_PASSED');

title: The Hoverer
story: The Hover Sanctum guards its spells behind invisible barriers. A simple click reveals nothing — only by hovering over the menu does the dropdown appear, and only then can the spell be selected. Master the hover, and the sanctum's powers are yours.
objective: Hover over '#menu-spells' to reveal the dropdown. Then click '#spell-lightning' to select Lightning Bolt. Verify '#selected-spell' contains 'Lightning Bolt'. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Use await page.locator('#menu-spells').hover() to simulate hovering — this triggers the CSS :hover state that reveals the dropdown.
After hovering, the dropdown is visible and #spell-lightning becomes clickable. Use await page.locator('#spell-lightning').click();
Read the result: const text = await page.locator('#selected-spell').textContent(); if (text.includes('Lightning Bolt')) console.log('LEVEL_PASSED');

title: The Session Keeper
story: The Arcane Registry demands login — but a true Session Keeper logs in once and saves their state. On the next visit, the registry recognises the saved session and shows the dashboard without requiring login again. Master storageState.
objective: Login with 'archmage'/'spellbound'. Save the session: const state = await context.storageState(). Create a new context with { storageState: state }. Navigate to the page in the new context and verify '#dashboard-panel' is visible without logging in. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: After login, save state: const state = await context1.storageState(); — this captures localStorage, sessionStorage, and cookies from context1.
Create new context with that state: const context2 = await browser.newContext({ storageState: state }); const page2 = await context2.newPage();

Navigate with page2 to the same URL. The page's JS reads localStorage on load and shows the dashboard directly. Check: if (await page2.locator('#dashboard-panel').isVisible()) console.log('LEVEL_PASSED');

title: The Header Mage
story: The Sealed Vault demands a magic key — not a password, but a request header. Every request from a Header Mage carries the X-Magic-Key. The vault's guardian inspects all incoming headers and only grants access to those who carry the key.
objective: Create a context with context.setExtraHTTPHeaders({'X-Magic-Key': 'open-sesame'}). Set up page.route to intercept '**/vault-treasure.json', inspect request.headers()['x-magic-key'], and fulfill with treasure data if correct. Click '#open-vault-btn', verify '#treasure-name' is visible. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Create context first: const context = await browser.newContext(); await context.setExtraHTTPHeaders({'X-Magic-Key': 'open-sesame'}); const page = await context.newPage();
In the route handler, check: const headers = request.headers(); if (headers['x-magic-key'] === 'open-sesame') { await route.fulfill({ json: { treasure: 'Dragon Heart Crystal', power: 9999 } }); }
After clicking #open-vault-btn and waiting, check if #vault-contents is visible. The page shows it when the fetch returns valid treasure data.

title: The Scroll Master
story: The Deep Archive hides its greatest relic far below the visible page. You cannot click what you cannot see — but a Scroll Master need not scroll manually. One command brings any element into view, no matter how deep it is buried.
objective: Navigate to the page. Use locator.scrollIntoViewIfNeeded() on '#buried-relic' to bring it into view. Then click '#claim-btn'. Verify '#claimed-msg' is visible. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Use await page.locator('#buried-relic').scrollIntoViewIfNeeded(); — this scrolls the page until the element enters the viewport.
Once in view, the element is interactable. Click: await page.click('#claim-btn');
Check visibility: const visible = await page.locator('#claimed-msg').isVisible(); if (visible) console.log('LEVEL_PASSED');

title: The Mouse Wizard
story: The Mana Conduit is a custom slider that rejects all fill() attempts. It was crafted by an ancient wizard who trusted only raw mouse control. To charge it, you must move the mouse to its track, press the mouse button, drag to the end, and release. Only then will it be fully charged.
objective: Get the bounding box of '#slider-track'. Use page.mouse.move(), page.mouse.down(), page.mouse.move() to the end (with steps), and page.mouse.up() to drag the slider to 100%. Verify '#mana-value' shows '100%'. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Get the bounding box first: const box = await page.locator('#slider-track').boundingBox(); This gives you { x, y, width, height }.
Simulate the drag: await page.mouse.move(box.x, box.y + box.height/2); await page.mouse.down(); await page.mouse.move(box.x + box.width, box.y + box.height/2, { steps: 20 }); await page.mouse.up();
The { steps: 20 } option fires 20 intermediate mousemove events for smooth dragging. Check: const val = await page.locator('#mana-value').textContent(); if (val === '100%') log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.

title: The Network Sentinel
story: The Arcane Observatory sends signals across the network. A Sentinel watches every transmission — not by intercepting, but by listening. Set your ears to the request and response events, let the signals pass unmodified, and report what you have observed.
objective: Set up page.on('request') and page.on('response') listeners BEFORE navigating. Click '#btn-prophecy'. Verify that a response event fired for a URL containing 'prophecy.json' with status 200. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Set up BEFORE goto(): page.on('response', res => responses.push({ url: res.url(), status: res.status() }));
After navigating and clicking '#btn-prophecy', wait briefly: await page.waitForTimeout(500);
Find the prophecy response: const r = responses.find(r => r.url.includes('prophecy.json')); if (r && r.status === 200) console.log('LEVEL_PASSED');

title: The Load Watcher
story: The Summoning Circle brings entities from the void one by one — each through a separate network request. A hasty tester asserts before all entities arrive and finds only partial results. A Load Watcher waits for the network to fall silent before making any claims.
objective: Click '#summon-btn' to start the ritual. Use page.waitForLoadState('networkidle') to wait for all async fetches to complete. Then assert all 4 entity cards appeared using toHaveCount(4). Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Click the button: await page.click('#summon-btn'); This starts 4 sequential async fetches with delays up to 2 seconds.
Wait for network silence: await page.waitForLoadState('networkidle'); This waits until no network requests have occurred for 500ms.
Then assert: await expect(page.locator('.entity-card.appeared')).toHaveCount(4); If all 4 arrived, log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.

title: The Mobile Shapeshifter
story: The Shapeshifter's page wears different forms for different visitors. Desktop users see a full navigation bar. Mobile users see a hamburger menu and a special mobile banner. A true Shapeshifter Tester can become any device — and assert what that device would see.
objective: Use const { devices } = require('playwright') and create a context with browser.newContext({ ...devices['iPhone 12'] }). Navigate to the page. Verify '#hamburger' is visible and '#layout-badge' contains 'Mobile Experience'. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.

title: The Form Enchanter
story: The Spell Registration Office demands precision. Checkboxes must be ticked, dropdowns chosen with care. Only those who master check(), uncheck(), and selectOption() may earn their certification.
objective: Check the #fire-mastery and #ice-mastery checkboxes. Select 'Archmage' from the #rank-select dropdown. Verify inputValue() returns 'Archmage'. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Use locator.check() to check a checkbox — it only checks if not already checked. Use locator.uncheck() to reverse it.
locator.selectOption('Archmage') selects the option whose value or text matches 'Archmage'.
locator.inputValue() returns the current value of an input or select element as a string. Compare it to verify the selection.

title: The Element Oracle
story: The Crystal Archive stores secrets deep within each element — data attributes invisible to the eye, computed styles hidden in the cascade. Only locator.evaluate() can pierce the veil and retrieve the raw truth.
objective: Use locator('#power-crystal').evaluate(el => el.dataset.power) to read the data-power attribute. Use locator('#spell-name').evaluate(el => el.textContent.trim()) to get its text. If power is '9000' and name includes 'Ancient', log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: locator.evaluate(el => ...) runs a function in the browser context with the matched DOM element as its argument.
Access data attributes via el.dataset.propertyName (camelCase) — so data-power becomes el.dataset.power.
Compare: if (power === '9000' && name.includes('Ancient')) console.log('LEVEL_PASSED');

title: The State Warden
story: The Locked Vault guards its secrets behind disabled gates, hidden runes, and sealed inscriptions. Not every truth needs an assertion — some elements reveal their state through direct boolean queries.
objective: Check isEnabled() on #locked-gate (should be false), isHidden() on #secret-rune (should be true), isEditable() on #sealed-input (should be false). If all three match, log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: locator.isEnabled() returns true if the element is not disabled. A button with the disabled attribute returns false.
locator.isHidden() returns true if the element has display:none, visibility:hidden, or is otherwise invisible.
locator.isEditable() returns true if the element is an input/textarea that is not readonly and not disabled. A readonly input returns false.

title: The Locator Alchemist
story: In the Spell Matrix, elements overlap and multiply. A button may be many things at once. The Locator Alchemist combines two queries into one unstoppable force with .and(), and casts a wide net with .or().
objective: Use page.getByRole('button').and(page.getByText('Fire Strike')) to find the Fire Strike button and verify its text. Use page.locator('.spell').or(page.locator('.rune')) to find all 6 combined items. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: locator.and(otherLocator) narrows down results — the element must match BOTH locators. Like an intersection.
locator.or(otherLocator) broadens results — the element must match EITHER locator. Like a union.
Count with await allItems.count() — there are 3 .spell and 3 .rune elements, totalling 6.

title: The Focus Keeper
story: The Arcane Portal Form can only be navigated by a true keyboard warrior. No mouse shall touch these fields. Focus must be given, then passed through Tab — and only the one who knows where focus lands shall unlock the portal.
objective: Focus #realm-input with locator.focus(). Press Tab twice with page.keyboard.press('Tab'). Evaluate document.activeElement.id — if it equals 'power-input', log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: locator.focus() programmatically focuses an element — equivalent to clicking it without triggering a click event.
page.keyboard.press('Tab') moves focus to the next focusable element in DOM order.
page.evaluate(() => document.activeElement.id) returns the id of the currently focused element. Two Tabs from #realm-input lands on #power-input.

title: The Condition Oracle
story: The Mana Crystal charges itself over time, ticking upward every 600ms. You cannot wait for a selector — there is no selector to wait for. Only a custom condition, born from your own predicate, can know when the mana is ready.
objective: Use page.waitForFunction(() => parseInt(document.getElementById('mana-counter').textContent) >= 5). After it resolves, read the counter value. If it is 5 or more, log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: page.waitForFunction(fn) polls the provided function in the browser context until it returns a truthy value.
The function runs in the browser — use standard DOM APIs like document.getElementById() inside it.
After waitForFunction resolves, the condition is guaranteed to have been true. Read the counter with locator.textContent() and parse it with parseInt().

hints: page.waitForFunction(fn) polls the provided function in the browser context until it returns a truthy value.
The function runs in the browser — use standard DOM APIs like document.getElementById() inside it.

title: The API Summoner
story: The true API warrior needs no browser — no viewport, no DOM, no clicks. Armed only with Playwright's APIRequestContext, they speak directly to the server in the language of HTTP: GET, POST, JSON.
objective: Use chromium.request.newContext() to create an API context. GET /pages/level-57/grimoire.json. Verify response.ok() is true and body.spellCount === 5. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'. Dispose the context.
hints: Use playwright.request.newContext() (not chromium.request) to create a standalone HTTP client — no browser required. Set baseURL to avoid repeating the host.
await request.get(path) makes an HTTP GET. The response object has .ok() (boolean), .status() (number), .json() (parsed body), .text() (raw string).
await response.json() parses the response body as JSON. Check body.spellCount === 5, then dispose: await request.dispose().

title: The Trace Keeper
story: The Arcane Observatory captures every spell, every click, every network whisper. Playwright's trace recorder writes a full chronicle of the test — screenshots, DOM snapshots, and network logs in a single archive.
objective: Start tracing with context.tracing.start({ screenshots: true, snapshots: true }). Navigate to the page and click the button. Stop tracing with context.tracing.stop({ path: '/tmp/trace-58.zip' }). Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Call context.tracing.start() BEFORE creating pages or navigating — it must be active to capture early events.
{ screenshots: true, snapshots: true } captures visual screenshots and DOM snapshots at each action step.
context.tracing.stop({ path }) writes the trace zip file. Open it at trace.playwright.dev to replay your test.

title: The HAR Recorder
story: The Network Nexus hums with requests and responses. An HAR archive captures the full conversation — every URL, status code, header, and body — for later inspection, replay, or mocking.
objective: Create a context with recordHar: { path: '/tmp/network-59.har' }. Navigate to the level page (it makes fetch requests on load). Close the context to flush the HAR. Log 'LEVEL_PASSED'.
hints: Pass recordHar: { path: '...' } when creating the browser context — HAR recording starts immediately for all pages in that context.
The HAR file is only written when the context is closed (await context.close()). Closing the browser without closing the context first may not flush it.
The HAR file is a JSON archive you can open in browser DevTools (Network tab → Import HAR) to replay and inspect all recorded requests.

title: The Download Warden
story: Files fall from the sky. The Download Warden intercepts them using page.waitForEvent('download') — catching every file before it lands.
objective: Use page.waitForEvent('download') to intercept a file download.
hints: Use Promise.all([page.waitForEvent('download'), triggerAction()]) to avoid race conditions
download.suggestedFilename() returns the file name
download.path() returns the temporary file path after download completes

title: The Download Warden — saves file to disk
story: Once caught, the Warden saves the download to a specific path using download.saveAs().
objective: Save a downloaded file to disk using download.saveAs().
hints: download.saveAs(path) copies the file to the specified path
Use a /tmp/ path for temporary test files
The file is ready to read after saveAs() resolves

title: The Download Warden — reads download path
story: The Warden inspects the temporary path where the file was stored by the browser.
objective: Use download.path() to get the temporary file path.
hints: download.path() returns null if the download failed
The temporary path is managed by Playwright — use saveAs() to persist it
download.path() is async and returns a Promise

title: The Download Warden — reads suggested filename
story: The Warden reads the suggested filename from the download header before saving.
objective: Use download.suggestedFilename() to get the original file name.
hints: download.suggestedFilename() returns the filename from Content-Disposition or the URL
This is synchronous — no await needed
Use it to validate the file name before saving

title: The Download Warden — cancels a download
story: Not all files are welcome. The Warden cancels unwanted downloads using download.cancel().
objective: Cancel a download in progress using download.cancel().
hints: download.cancel() cancels the download and rejects the path promise
After cancelling, download.path() returns null
Useful for testing UI behaviour when a download is aborted

title: The WebSocket Watcher
story: Real-time connections flow through WebSockets. The Watcher listens on page.on('websocket') to observe every connection the page opens.
objective: Use page.on('websocket') to intercept a WebSocket connection.
hints: page.on('websocket', ws => { }) fires for every WebSocket created
ws.url() returns the WebSocket endpoint URL
ws.on('framesent', data => { }) and ws.on('framereceived', data => { }) monitor messages

title: The WebSocket Watcher — monitors sent frames
story: Every message sent through the socket is a frame. The Watcher tracks outgoing frames with ws.on('framesent').
objective: Listen to framesent events on a WebSocket connection.
hints: ws.on('framesent', frame => { frame.payload }) gives you the sent message
frame.payload is a string or Buffer
Set up the listener before the WebSocket is used to avoid missing messages

title: The WebSocket Watcher — monitors received frames
story: Incoming messages tell the story of the server response. The Watcher captures them with ws.on('framereceived').
objective: Listen to framereceived events on a WebSocket.
hints: ws.on('framereceived', frame => { }) fires for each incoming message
frame.payload is the message content
Combine with framesent to build a full message log

title: The WebSocket Watcher — detects WebSocket URL
story: The Watcher reads the WebSocket endpoint URL to verify the app is connecting to the right server.
objective: Read the URL of an intercepted WebSocket connection.
hints: ws.url() returns the full WebSocket URL
Use this to verify the correct endpoint is being used
Combine with an assertion to fail the test if the URL is wrong

title: The WebSocket Watcher — detects WebSocket close
story: Every connection eventually closes. The Watcher detects it with ws.on('close').
objective: Listen for the WebSocket close event.
hints: ws.on('close', () => { }) fires when the socket closes
The close event fires for both normal and abnormal closures
Useful for detecting unexpected disconnections in tests

title: The Bridge Builder
story: The Bridge Builder connects the Node.js world to the browser with page.exposeFunction() — making server-side functions callable from page scripts.
objective: Use page.exposeFunction() to expose a Node.js function to the browser.
hints: page.exposeFunction('name', fn) adds fn to window.name in the browser
The function can be async and returns a Promise in the browser
Call it from page.evaluate() or page scripts

title: The Bridge Builder — async exposed function
story: The bridge carries async cargo too. An exposed function can return a Promise, and the browser awaits it.
objective: Expose an async function and await its result in the browser.
hints: Async functions exposed via exposeFunction return Promises in the browser
Use await window.myFunc() in evaluate
This lets you call fs.readFile or database queries from the browser context

title: The Bridge Builder — exposes binding with handle
story: page.exposeBinding() is the advanced bridge — it receives a source object with the page and frame context alongside the arguments.
objective: Use page.exposeBinding() to expose a function that receives context info.
hints: page.exposeBinding('name', (source, ...args) => { source.page }) gives you the page reference
source.frame is the calling frame, source.page is the page
Use { handle: true } option to get JSHandle arguments instead of plain values

title: The Bridge Builder — exposes function on context
story: The bridge can span all pages in a context. context.exposeFunction() makes the function available in every new page.
objective: Use context.exposeFunction() to expose a function across all pages.
hints: context.exposeFunction() works just like page.exposeFunction() but for all pages
Must be called before creating pages (or they won't have the function)
Useful for shared utilities like logging or ID generation

title: The Bridge Builder — reads file from browser context
story: The Bridge Builder's ultimate trick: reading a file from Node.js via a browser-triggered call.
objective: Use page.exposeFunction() to read a Node.js file from within page.evaluate().
hints: Expose fs.readFileSync wrapped in an async function
Call it from evaluate to get file contents in the browser context
This pattern lets tests read config files from within browser scripts

title: The Spell Inscriber
story: Some magic must be cast before the page awakens. The Spell Inscriber uses page.addInitScript() to inject code that runs before any page scripts load.
objective: Use page.addInitScript() to inject a script that runs before page load.
hints: page.addInitScript(fn) runs fn in the browser before the page scripts execute
The function runs in the browser context — no Node.js access
Use it to mock globals, override APIs, or set up test state before load

title: The Spell Inscriber — passes args to init script
story: The Inscriber carries data into the scroll. page.addInitScript() accepts a { content } string or a function with an arg parameter.
objective: Pass a value into page.addInitScript() via script content.
hints: page.addInitScript({ content: `window.X = ${value}` }) lets you template values in
For object args use JSON.stringify()
This runs before the page loads so the values are ready for the app immediately

title: The Spell Inscriber — mocks a browser API
story: The Inscriber replaces built-in browser APIs before the page can use them — mocking Date.now() or Math.random() for deterministic tests.
objective: Use page.addInitScript() to override a built-in browser API.
hints: Override Date by setting window.Date in the init script
Math.random can be replaced with () => 0.5 for deterministic tests
This is more reliable than hooking after load because app code runs after the init script

title: The Spell Inscriber — applies to all pages via context
story: The Inscriber can brand all pages in a context. context.addInitScript() applies to every page opened in that context.
objective: Use context.addInitScript() so the script runs in every page of the context.
hints: context.addInitScript() must be called before opening pages
All pages in the context will have the script injected
Useful for test setup that should apply globally

title: The Spell Inscriber — injects a script from file
story: Scripts can live in files. The Inscriber loads them from disk using the path option.
objective: Use page.addInitScript() with a file path to inject a script.
hints: page.addInitScript({ path: './setup.js' }) loads from a file
Write the script to /tmp first using fs.writeFileSync
Relative paths are resolved from the current working directory

title: The HTML Archivist
story: The HTML Archivist captures the entire DOM as a string using page.content() — useful for snapshot testing, scraping, and debugging.
objective: Use page.content() to get the full HTML of the page.
hints: page.content() returns the full serialised HTML as a string
It includes the <html>, <head> and <body> tags
Useful for comparing page state before and after an action

title: The HTML Archivist — checks for specific element in HTML
story: The Archivist searches the raw HTML string for a specific element — a quick way to verify server-rendered content.
objective: Check that page.content() contains a specific HTML element.
hints: page.content() returns a string — use .includes() to search it
Useful for verifying that SSR rendered an expected element
The content reflects the current DOM state, not the original HTML source

title: The HTML Archivist — compares content before and after
story: The Archivist records the HTML before and after an action to verify the DOM changed.
objective: Capture page.content() before and after an action and compare the results.
hints: Call page.content() before the action, then again after
Compare the two strings to verify something changed
This is useful for smoke-testing dynamic content

title: The HTML Archivist — measures content length
story: The length of the HTML indicates the richness of the page. The Archivist measures it to detect empty pages.
objective: Assert that page.content() returns a string with meaningful length.
hints: A blank page has very short HTML — typically < 200 chars
Real pages are usually > 500 chars
page.content().length gives the byte size of the serialized DOM

title: The HTML Archivist — uses innerHTML for a specific element
story: When the full page is too much, the Archivist uses locator.innerHTML() to read just one element's markup.
objective: Use locator.innerHTML() to get the inner HTML of a specific element.
hints: locator.innerHTML() returns the inner HTML as a string
Different from textContent() — it includes child tags
Use it to verify dynamic template rendering

title: The PDF Scribe
story: The PDF Scribe freezes pages into permanent documents using page.pdf() — generating reports and invoices for testing.
objective: Use page.pdf() to generate a PDF buffer from the current page.
hints: page.pdf() only works in headless Chromium — not Firefox or WebKit
It returns a Buffer containing the PDF data
Pass { path } to save directly to disk

title: The PDF Scribe — saves PDF to disk
story: The Scribe writes the PDF to a file using the path option so it persists after the test.
objective: Use page.pdf({ path }) to save the PDF directly to a file.
hints: page.pdf({ path: '/tmp/page.pdf' }) saves to disk
When path is provided, the method still returns the Buffer
Verify the file exists with fs.existsSync()

title: The PDF Scribe — sets page format
story: A4, Letter, A3 — the Scribe chooses the paper format for the PDF.
objective: Generate a PDF with a specific paper format using page.pdf({ format }).
hints: Supported formats: Letter, Legal, Tabloid, Ledger, A0–A6
page.pdf({ format: 'A4' }) generates A4-sized PDF
Combine format with margin for professional layouts

title: The PDF Scribe — prints background graphics
story: Background colors and images are hidden in PDFs by default. The Scribe enables them with printBackground.
objective: Use page.pdf({ printBackground: true }) to include CSS backgrounds.
hints: printBackground: true enables CSS background colors and images in the PDF
Useful for branded reports with colored headers
Default is false — backgrounds are stripped

title: The PDF Scribe — sets margin
story: Professional PDFs have proper margins. The Scribe sets top, bottom, left and right margins.
objective: Use page.pdf({ margin }) to add margins to the PDF output.
hints: page.pdf({ margin: { top: '1cm', bottom: '1cm' } }) sets margins
Values can be in cm, mm, px or in
Margins affect page breaks and content overflow

title: The Offline Oracle
story: The Offline Oracle severs the network connection using context.setOffline(true) — testing how the app behaves when the internet disappears.
objective: Use context.setOffline(true) to simulate a network outage.
hints: context.setOffline(true) makes all network requests fail immediately
context.setOffline(false) restores connectivity
Test offline UI states like "No connection" banners

title: The Offline Oracle — restores connectivity
story: After the outage, the Oracle restores the connection and verifies the app recovers.
objective: Toggle offline mode off using context.setOffline(false) and verify the page loads.
hints: Set offline, then set back to false, then try navigating
Test the reload or retry logic in your app
context.setOffline() affects all pages in the context

title: The Offline Oracle — checks offline error type
story: When offline, navigation throws a specific error. The Oracle catches and identifies it.
objective: Catch the navigation error thrown when context.setOffline(true) is active.
hints: The error message typically contains "net::ERR_INTERNET_DISCONNECTED" or similar
Wrap the goto in try/catch to handle it gracefully
Use error.message to inspect what kind of failure occurred

title: The Offline Oracle — tests cached content
story: The Oracle loads a page first, then goes offline to check if cached content still renders.
objective: Load a page while online, go offline, then reload to test cache behaviour.
hints: Service workers and browser cache may serve content when offline
After going offline, page.reload() may still show content from cache
Test the difference between cached and uncached offline states

title: The Offline Oracle — blocks specific resources
story: More surgical than full offline mode — the Oracle blocks specific domains using page.route() while letting others through.
objective: Use page.route() to block requests to a specific origin instead of using setOffline.
hints: page.route('**/api/**', route => route.abort()) blocks all API calls
This is more targeted than context.setOffline() which blocks everything
Combine with route.fulfill() to return a "network error" response

title: The State Inspector
story: The State Inspector checks whether elements are hidden, disabled, or editable — without making assertions that fail tests.
objective: Use locator.isHidden() to check if an element is not visible.
hints: locator.isHidden() returns true if the element is hidden or not in the DOM
isHidden() is the opposite of isVisible()
Both return a boolean — use them in if-else for conditional logic

title: The State Inspector — isDisabled check
story: Disabled elements reject user input. The Inspector verifies the enabled state before attempting to interact.
objective: Use locator.isDisabled() to check if a form element is disabled.
hints: locator.isDisabled() returns true if the element has a disabled attribute
isDisabled() is the inverse of isEnabled()
Use this before click() or fill() to avoid errors on disabled elements

title: The State Inspector — isEditable check
story: Not all inputs accept changes. The Inspector checks editability before typing.
objective: Use locator.isEditable() to check if an input can be edited.
hints: locator.isEditable() returns false for disabled or readonly inputs
Use it to conditionally fill or skip an element
An element is editable if it is enabled and not readonly

title: The State Inspector — combines state checks
story: The Inspector runs all three checks — visible, enabled, editable — before interacting with an element.
objective: Check isVisible, isEnabled and isEditable on the same element.
hints: Run all three checks in parallel using Promise.all() for speed
A fully interactive element is visible AND enabled AND editable
This pre-check pattern prevents flaky test failures on dynamic forms

title: The State Inspector — isChecked for checkboxes
story: The Inspector reads the checked state of checkboxes and radio buttons without toggling them.
objective: Use locator.isChecked() to read the current state of a checkbox.
hints: locator.isChecked() returns true if the checkbox or radio is selected
Different from isEnabled() — a checked element can still be disabled
Use before check()/uncheck() to verify current state

title: The Text Harvester
story: The Text Harvester gathers text from every matching element at once using locator.allTextContents() — no loops needed.
objective: Use locator.allTextContents() to get text from all matching elements.
hints: locator.allTextContents() returns an array of strings
Each string is the textContent of one matching element
Does NOT retry — for retry behaviour use expect(locator).toHaveCount()

title: The Text Harvester — allInnerTexts for visible text
story: innerText respects CSS visibility — allInnerTexts() returns what the user actually sees, skipping hidden content.
objective: Use locator.allInnerTexts() to get visible text from all matching elements.
hints: allInnerTexts() respects CSS — hidden elements return empty strings
textContent includes hidden text; innerText does not
More accurate for testing what the user actually reads

title: The Text Harvester — finds specific text in list
story: The Harvester collects all item texts and checks if a target value is in the harvest.
objective: Use allTextContents() and Array.includes() to find a specific text.
hints: allTextContents() returns an array you can use with .includes(), .find(), .filter()
Trim whitespace with .map(t => t.trim()) for reliable matching
This is faster than querying each element individually

title: The Text Harvester — counts items by text
story: The Harvester counts how many elements contain a target word — revealing duplicate content or repeated data.
objective: Use allTextContents() to count elements containing a specific string.
hints: texts.filter(t => t.includes('word')).length gives the count
Combine with allTextContents() for a one-liner count
Works well for verifying search result counts

title: The Text Harvester — sorted text comparison
story: The Harvester verifies sorted lists by comparing allTextContents() to the expected sorted order.
objective: Get all item texts and verify they are in sorted order.
hints: Get texts, make a sorted copy, then compare with JSON.stringify()
texts.every((t, i) => i === 0 || t >= texts[i-1]) checks ascending order
Useful for testing sort functionality in tables or lists

title: The Geometry Sage
story: Position and size matter. The Geometry Sage reads element coordinates using locator.boundingBox() — verifying layout and overlap.
objective: Use locator.boundingBox() to get the position and size of an element.
hints: boundingBox() returns { x, y, width, height } in pixels
Returns null if the element is not visible
Coordinates are relative to the viewport

title: The Geometry Sage — checks element position
story: The Sage verifies an element appears in the correct region of the page — top, bottom, left or right.
objective: Assert that an element's bounding box places it in the correct area.
hints: box.x is the left edge, box.y is the top edge
Elements at the top of the page have small y values
Compare box.x and box.y against expected layout constraints

title: The Geometry Sage — checks element size
story: Size conveys importance. The Sage verifies that key elements are not collapsed to zero dimensions.
objective: Assert that an element has a non-zero width and height.
hints: A visible element always has width > 0 and height > 0
Collapsed elements (display:none or visibility:hidden) return null from boundingBox()
Use this to detect layout regressions

title: The Geometry Sage — compares two element positions
story: The Sage verifies relative layout: element A should appear above element B.
objective: Compare bounding boxes of two elements to verify their relative positions.
hints: Get both bounding boxes and compare their y values
boxA.y < boxB.y means A appears above B on the page
This pattern is great for testing visual hierarchy

title: The Geometry Sage — null box for hidden element
story: The Sage knows that invisible elements have no geometry. boundingBox() returns null for hidden elements.
objective: Verify that boundingBox() returns null for a hidden element.
hints: Elements with display:none return null from boundingBox()
Elements with visibility:hidden also return null
Always null-check boundingBox() before using its properties

title: The Event Conjurer
story: The Event Conjurer summons any DOM event directly using locator.dispatchEvent() — no need to physically interact with the element.
objective: Use locator.dispatchEvent() to fire a custom DOM event.
hints: locator.dispatchEvent('click') fires a click event without the actionability checks
Pass event properties: locator.dispatchEvent('click', { bubbles: true })
Use it for events Playwright doesn't have native methods for (e.g., 'input', 'change')

title: The Event Conjurer — dispatches custom event
story: Beyond standard browser events, the Conjurer creates fully custom events with detail payloads.
objective: Use dispatchEvent() to fire a CustomEvent with a detail payload.
hints: dispatchEvent('custom-event', { bubbles: true, detail: { value: 42 } }) fires a custom event
Listen for it with addEventListener in an init script or evaluate
CustomEvent detail is accessible via event.detail in the handler

title: The Event Conjurer — dispatches input event
story: The input event is not always triggered by fill(). The Conjurer fires it manually to update reactive frameworks.
objective: Use dispatchEvent('input') to trigger the input event on a form field.
hints: dispatchEvent('input') fires the native input event
Useful for React/Vue/Angular which listen on the input event for reactivity
Combine with .fill() + dispatchEvent('input') for full reactivity trigger

title: The Event Conjurer — dispatches mouse events
story: The Conjurer fires mouseenter and mouseleave for hover states that click() alone cannot trigger.
objective: Use dispatchEvent() to fire mouseenter on an element.
hints: dispatchEvent('mouseenter') fires on the element without moving the mouse
Useful for testing CSS :hover states or JS mouseover handlers
Combine with mouseleave to test hover toggling

title: The Event Conjurer — dispatches keyboard event
story: keydown, keyup and keypress can be dispatched directly on any element.
objective: Use dispatchEvent('keydown') with a key property on a focused element.
hints: dispatchEvent('keydown', { key: 'Enter', keyCode: 13 }) fires Enter
The element should be focused before dispatching keyboard events
Useful for testing key-combo shortcuts

title: The Keystroke Chronicler
story: Some apps react to every keystroke. The Keystroke Chronicler uses pressSequentially() to type character by character, firing key events for each.
objective: Use locator.pressSequentially() to type text one character at a time.
hints: pressSequentially(text) fires keydown, keypress, input, keyup for each character
Different from fill() which sets the value directly without key events
Use it to test autocomplete, character counters, or live validation

title: The Keystroke Chronicler — with delay between keystrokes
story: Slow typists fire events with gaps. The Chronicler adds a delay between each keystroke for realistic simulation.
objective: Use pressSequentially() with a delay option between keystrokes.
hints: pressSequentially(text, { delay: 50 }) adds 50ms between each character
Useful for testing debounced inputs or rate-limited searches
Higher delays slow the test — keep it under 100ms in CI

title: The Keystroke Chronicler — fires input events per character
story: The Chronicler proves that pressSequentially() fires an input event for each character, enabling testing of character-by-character handlers.
objective: Verify that pressSequentially() fires the input event for each character typed.
hints: Listen for input events with page.evaluate before typing
Count the events to verify one per character
Compare with fill() which fires only one input event

title: The Keystroke Chronicler — clears before typing
story: Existing text must be cleared before the Chronicler can begin. locator.clear() empties the field first.
objective: Use locator.clear() to empty an input before using pressSequentially().
hints: locator.clear() removes all text from an input or textarea
It fires the input event — different from page.evaluate(() => el.value = '')
Chain clear() then pressSequentially() for full control

title: The Keystroke Chronicler — blur after typing
story: After typing, the Chronicler triggers blur to complete validation — just like a real user moving to the next field.
objective: Use locator.blur() to remove focus from an input after typing.
hints: locator.blur() removes focus and triggers the blur event

Chain: fill() → blur() → assert on validation message

title: The Handle Keeper
story: Some objects cannot be serialised. The Handle Keeper uses page.evaluateHandle() to get a JSHandle — a reference to a browser object that stays in the browser.
objective: Use page.evaluateHandle() to get a JSHandle for a DOM element.
hints: evaluateHandle() returns a JSHandle (or ElementHandle for DOM nodes)
Unlike evaluate(), the return value is not serialised — it stays in the browser
Use handle.evaluate() or handle.asElement() to work with it

title: The Handle Keeper — gets window object
story: The window object lives in the browser. The Handle Keeper captures a JSHandle to it for inspection.
objective: Use page.evaluateHandle(() => window) to get a handle to the window object.
hints: page.evaluateHandle(() => window) gives you a handle to the global object
Use handle.getProperty('propertyName') to read individual window properties
handle.getProperties() returns all enumerable properties as a Map

title: The Handle Keeper — passes handle back to evaluate
story: A JSHandle can be passed back into evaluate() — letting you run multiple operations on the same browser object without round-trips.
objective: Pass a JSHandle as an argument to page.evaluate().
hints: page.evaluate((el) => el.textContent, handle) passes the handle as an argument
This avoids re-querying the element on each call
Dispose handles after use with handle.dispose()

title: The Handle Keeper — converts to ElementHandle

objective: Use handle.asElement() to convert a JSHandle to an ElementHandle.
hints: handle.asElement() returns an ElementHandle if the handle is a DOM element
Returns null if the handle is not an Element
ElementHandle has methods like click(), fill(), screenshot()

title: The Handle Keeper — disposes handles to prevent leaks
story: Handles hold browser references. The Handle Keeper always disposes them after use to prevent memory leaks.
objective: Use handle.dispose() to release a JSHandle after use.
hints: handle.dispose() releases the browser-side reference
Undisposed handles accumulate memory — always dispose in finally blocks
After dispose(), using the handle throws an error

title: The Script Sorcerer
story: The Script Sorcerer conjures new scripts into an already-loaded page using page.addScriptTag() — injecting utilities, polyfills, or test helpers.
objective: Use page.addScriptTag() to inject a script into the page at runtime.
hints: page.addScriptTag({ content: 'window.X = 1' }) injects inline JS
page.addScriptTag({ url: '...' }) loads an external script
page.addScriptTag({ path: './file.js' }) loads from disk

title: The Script Sorcerer — injects a style tag

objective: Use page.addStyleTag() to inject CSS into the page.
hints: page.addStyleTag({ content: 'body { color: red }' }) injects inline CSS
page.addStyleTag({ url: '...' }) loads an external stylesheet
Useful for testing accessibility with high contrast or custom themes

title: The Script Sorcerer — injects script from file

objective: Use page.addScriptTag({ path }) to load a local script file.
hints: Write a file with fs.writeFileSync first, then load it with addScriptTag
The path is relative to the current working directory
Good for injecting large test helpers or libraries

title: The Script Sorcerer — injects style from file

hints: Write a CSS file with fs.writeFileSync

Useful for injecting test-specific styles without modifying the app

title: The Script Sorcerer — injects multiple scripts in sequence

objective: Inject two scripts sequentially so the second can use the first.
hints: Await each addScriptTag before the next
The second script can access window properties set by the first
Order matters — scripts execute in injection order

title: The Event Spy Forge
story: Callbacks carry meaning. The Event Spy Forge mounts components with cy.spy() wired directly into event handler props — so you can assert not just that a function was called, but exactly what arguments it received.
objective: Use cy.spy() as a component prop to verify event handler callbacks are called with the correct arguments when the user interacts with the component.
hints: cy.spy() returns a sinon spy — pass it directly as a prop or wrap it in an arrow function
Use .as('name') on the spy so you can reference it later with cy.get('@name')
cy.get('@spy').its('lastCall.args.0') accesses the first argument of the most recent call
cy.get('@spy').should('have.been.calledWith', value) asserts the spy was called with that exact argument at least once

title: The Router Realm
story: Components that navigate are useless without a router. The Router Realm wraps mounted components in a MemoryRouter — giving Link, NavLink, and useNavigate the context they need to render and respond correctly in isolation.
objective: Mount components that use React Router (Link, NavLink, useNavigate) by wrapping them in MemoryRouter, and assert that navigation and active states work correctly.
hints: Wrap any component that uses Link, NavLink, or useNavigate with <MemoryRouter> inside cy.mount()
Use initialEntries={['/path']} on MemoryRouter to set the starting URL for the component
NavLink applies its active class/style when its to prop matches the current MemoryRouter path

title: The Redux Sanctum
story: Redux-connected components see nothing without a store. The Redux Sanctum wraps mounted components in a pre-loaded Provider — giving useSelector and useDispatch a real store to read from and write to.
objective: Mount Redux-connected components by wrapping them in a Provider with a pre-configured store, and assert that the component renders from state and dispatches actions correctly.
hints: Use a factory function like makeStore(preloadedState) so each test gets its own isolated store
Wrap the component in <Provider store={store}> inside cy.mount() — same pattern as production code
Never share a single store instance across tests — state mutations in one test will corrupt the next

title: The Context Weaver
story: React Context is invisible in isolation. The Context Weaver wraps mounted components in their required context providers — feeding theme, locale, user, or any shared value directly into the component without a full app stack.
objective: Mount components that consume React Context by wrapping them in the appropriate Provider, and assert the component renders correctly based on different context values.
hints: Wrap the component in <MyContext.Provider value={...}> inside cy.mount() to inject any context value
Mount the same component twice with different context values to test all branches in one describe block
For multiple contexts, nest providers: outer context wraps inner context wraps the component

title: The Mount Spellbook
story: Repeating providers in every test is noise. The Mount Spellbook centralises all wrappers into a custom cy.mount() command — so every component test starts with router, store, and context already wired up, with zero boilerplate.
objective: Create a custom Cypress mount command that wraps components with all required providers, and use it to simplify component tests across multiple scenarios.
hints: Define Cypress.Commands.add('mountWithProviders', ...) in cypress/support/component.jsx so it is available in every component test file
Accept an options object with named fields (storeState, initialEntries) so callers only specify what they need to override
Sensible defaults in the destructuring (storeState = {}, initialEntries = ['/']) mean callers can omit options entirely

clearLocalStorage() in beforeEach ensures each test starts unauthenticated

title: The Truthiness Tribunal
story: The Oracle demands proof. Some values are truthy, some falsy, some null, some undefined. Use Chai's truthiness assertions to pass judgement on each one.
objective: Use be.ok, be.true, be.false, be.null, and be.undefined on wrapped values to complete all assertions.
hints: be.ok is truthy check — 1, 'hello', [], {} all pass; 0, '', null, undefined, false all fail
be.true is strict (=== true), not just truthy — cy.wrap(1).should('not.be.true') passes
Chain not before any assertion to negate it: .should('not.be.null')

title: The Equality Enchantment

objective: Use equal (strict ===), eql / deep.equal (deep comparison), and not.equal on wrapped values.
hints: equal uses === (strict), so cy.wrap({}).should('equal', {}) FAILS — different references
eql does deep value comparison, so cy.wrap({a:1}).should('eql', {a:1}) PASSES
deep.equal is an alias for eql — either works

title: The Comparison Crucible
story: The guild's ranking system demands precise comparisons. A hero's power level must exceed a minimum, fall below a maximum, and sit within an acceptable range.
objective: Use greaterThan (gt), at.least (gte), lessThan (lt), at.most (lte), and within on wrapped numbers.
hints: greaterThan and gt are aliases — pick whichever reads better
at.least means >= (greater than OR equal), so cy.wrap(85).should('be.at.least', 85) passes
within is inclusive on both ends: within(40, 50) means 40 <= x <= 50

objective: Use be.a / be.an (typeof check), instanceof (class check), and oneOf (membership check).

instanceof checks the prototype chain, not typeof
oneOf uses strict equality, so cy.wrap('Mage').should('be.oneOf', ['mage']) fails (case-sensitive)

title: The Change Watcher
story: Magic flows. Numbers shift. The Change Watcher observes mutations — does a function increase, decrease, or change a value? Chai's change assertions capture state transitions.
objective: Use change, increase, and decrease to assert that a function mutates an object property.
hints: change, increase, decrease take (fn, object, propertyName) — they call fn and compare before/after
increase requires the value to go UP (not just change), decrease requires it to go DOWN
These wrap a function, so pass the function reference without calling it: cy.wrap(fn).should('change', ...)

title: The Satisfaction Rite
story: When standard assertions fall short, the Satisfaction Rite accepts any custom predicate. Define the rule yourself — if the function returns true, the test passes.
objective: Use satisfy (custom predicate function) and respondTo (object has a method) to write flexible assertions.
hints: satisfy takes a function that receives the subject — return true to pass, false to fail
respondTo checks if the object has a method with that name (own or prototype)
You can combine satisfy with not: .should('not.satisfy', fn) for inverse predicate checks

title: The DOM Navigator
story: The guild hall's structure is complex — rooms within rooms, sections within sections. The DOM Navigator maps the descendants of each container and matches elements by CSS selector.
objective: Use match (CSS selector check), have.descendants, and be.empty to inspect DOM tree structure.
hints: match checks if the element itself matches the selector — like .matches() in native JS
have.descendants checks if any descendant elements match the selector (like .find())
Combine .match with compound selectors: .character.active checks for both classes

title: The Visibility Veil
story: Some elements lurk in shadow — hidden by CSS, tucked off-screen, or veiled by invisible parents. The Visibility Veil reveals what is truly seen and what is merely present.
objective: Use be.visible and be.hidden to check whether elements are actually rendered on screen.
hints: be.visible checks CSS visibility — an element hidden with display:none, visibility:hidden, or off-screen returns be.hidden
An element can exist in DOM but be.hidden — existence and visibility are separate
If a parent is hidden, all children are also be.hidden even if they have no hidden styles themselves

title: The Call Counter
story: Did the spell fire once or twice? The Call Counter attaches invisible trackers to window functions, then counts exactly how many times they were invoked.
objective: Use cy.spy() and cy.stub(), then assert call counts with calledOnce, calledTwice, calledThrice, and have.callCount.
hints: cy.spy() wraps and tracks but still calls the original function; cy.stub() replaces it entirely
calledOnce, calledTwice, calledThrice are sugar — have.callCount(N) works for any number
Wrap the spy/stub with cy.wrap() to use Cypress retry-ability: cy.wrap(spy).should(...)

objective: Use calledWith, calledBefore, calledAfter, and calledWithNew to inspect spy call details.
hints: calledWith checks if the spy was EVER called with those args (not necessarily the last call)
calledBefore(otherSpy) checks call ORDER — both must have been called at least once
calledWithNew checks if the function was called using the 'new' keyword

title: The Nested Chronicles
story: Mocha is the test framework Cypress uses under the hood. Every describe(), context(), and it() you write is Mocha. Learn to nest suites, use context() for conditions, and organise tests clearly.
objective: Write a two-level nested test suite using describe(), context(), and it() blocks with at least one assertion in each test.
hints: context() is a pure alias for describe() — they are identical in behaviour
Tests can be nested as deeply as you want — each describe creates a new scope
The suite name appears in the Cypress run output, so use descriptive strings

title: The Suite Sentinels
story: before() and after() are the gatekeepers of the suite — running once before all tests begin and once after all tests end. Use them for expensive setup and teardown that only needs to happen once.
objective: Use before() to set up shared state and after() to verify final state. Both must run successfully.
hints: before() runs once — shared state mutations inside tests persist to subsequent tests
after() runs even if tests fail (unless --bail is set)
Use before() for expensive setup like seeding data; use beforeEach() when each test needs a fresh start

title: The Test Groundskeeper
story: beforeEach() and afterEach() are the Groundskeepers — resetting state before every single test and cleaning up after. They ensure each test starts fresh and isolated.
objective: Use beforeEach() to visit a page and set up state, and afterEach() to log results. Write three independent tests that each rely on the fresh setup.
hints: beforeEach() in a parent describe also runs for tests in nested describe blocks
afterEach() runs even when the test fails — great for screenshots or logging
Each it() gets a completely independent page state because cy.visit() runs before every test

title: The Skipped Scrolls

objective: Use it.skip() to mark tests as pending and this.retries() to configure retry logic. All non-skipped tests must pass.
hints: it.skip() and xit() are identical — both mark the test as pending
this.retries(N) requires a regular function() not an arrow () => because it needs 'this'
describe.skip() skips ALL tests inside that suite block

objective: Use cy.get('body').then($body => { if ($body.find(...).length) { ... } }) to handle the random modal gracefully, then continue the test regardless.
hints: cy.get('body').then($body => ...) gives you a synchronous jQuery snapshot of the DOM
Check $body.find('#el').css('display') !== 'none' or $body.find('#el').length > 0
The key insight: don't assert existence BEFORE the conditional — query inside .then() where you already have the snapshot

title: The URL Puppeteer
story: The safest conditional is no conditional at all — control the state yourself before the test runs. Pass ?campaign=A or ?campaign=B in the URL and the page renders deterministically every time.
objective: Use cy.visit() with query parameters to deterministically set page state, eliminating the need for DOM conditionals entirely.
hints: cy.visit('/page?key=value') is the cleanest way to set state — no DOM conditionals needed
URLSearchParams is a native browser API that safely encodes query strings
This pattern mirrors real-world A/B testing: you control which variant runs by passing a param

title: The Cookie Oracle
story: Cookies hold truth. Instead of guessing what the UI will show, read the cookie first — then you know exactly what state to expect. Set a cookie before visiting and the page renders predictably.
objective: Use cy.setCookie() to set state before visiting, and cy.getCookie() to read and branch on cookie values inside tests.
hints: Set cookies with cy.setCookie() BEFORE cy.visit() — cookies must exist when the page loads
cy.getCookie() returns null if the cookie doesn't exist — check for this before reading .value
cy.clearCookies() in beforeEach ensures each test starts with a clean slate

title: The Request Scout
story: The most reliable source of truth is the server itself. Before touching the UI, send a cy.request() to the API — use the authoritative response to know exactly what the page will show, with zero guesswork.
objective: Use cy.request() to query server state before the UI loads, then use the response data to drive test assertions deterministically.
hints: cy.request() is synchronous in the Cypress command queue — it completes before the next command runs
The .then(response => ...) callback gives you the full response: status, body, headers
Real pattern: cy.request() your auth endpoint first, get the user role, then decide which UI flows to test

title: The Stability Ritual
story: A test that passes once might be hiding non-determinism. The Stability Ritual uses Cypress._.times() to run the same test dozens of times in one spec — if it fails even once, the instability is exposed.
objective: Use Cypress._.times() to run repeated test iterations, and write tests that handle non-deterministic UI (the random modal) reliably on every run.
hints: Cypress._.times(N, i => ...) is evaluated at parse time — it creates N separate it() blocks in the Cypress UI
If a test flickers across runs, the conditional handling inside is incomplete or wrong
URL param tests should NEVER flicker — if they do, the page JavaScript has a bug

title: The Request Forge
story: The requests you send tell the server who you are. The Request Forge teaches you to intercept outgoing requests and reshape them before they ever reach the server — swap headers, change the body, or add custom tokens on the fly.
objective: Use cy.intercept() with a handler function to modify request headers and inspect the full interception object including request URL, method, and response body.
hints: cy.intercept() with a handler function (req) => { ... } gives you the live request object to modify before it is sent
req.headers, req.body, req.url, and req.method are all writable inside the handler
The interception object from cy.wait("@alias") has .request and .response sub-objects with full details
Use req.reply({ statusCode, body }) inside the handler to return a custom response immediately without hitting the server

title: The Response Sculptor
story: Sometimes you do not want to replace a real server response — you want to tweak it. The Response Sculptor uses req.continue() to let the real request fly, then intercepts the response before it hits the browser.
objective: Use cy.intercept() with req.continue(res => ...) to modify a real server response — changing the body, status code, and headers — without fully stubbing it.
hints: req.continue(res => ...) sends the real request and gives you the response to modify before the browser sees it
res.body, res.statusCode, and res.headers are all writable inside the callback
Unlike full stubbing, req.continue() still validates that your real server returns a response
Call req.continue() without a callback to simply pass the request through with no modification

title: The Delay Weaver
story: Not all networks are fast. The Delay Weaver simulates sluggish servers and spotty connections — intercepting requests and injecting delays to verify your app handles loading states gracefully under pressure.
objective: Use cy.intercept() with a delay option to simulate slow network responses and assert that loading states and error states appear correctly.
hints: Add delay: N (milliseconds) to any static intercept response object to simulate slow networks
Your loading state UI must render synchronously — assert it immediately after cy.visit() before cy.wait()
Combine delay with statusCode and body in the same object to simulate real error scenarios
Pass { timeout: N } to cy.wait() when the delay is longer than Cypress's default 4000ms command timeout

title: The GraphQL Oracle
story: GraphQL uses a single endpoint for everything, making URL matching alone useless. The GraphQL Oracle teaches you to peer inside the request body and intercept by operationName — the true identity of each query or mutation.
objective: Use cy.intercept() with a handler function to match GraphQL operations by operationName in the POST body and stub responses for specific queries without affecting others.
hints: GraphQL always POSTs to the same URL — use req.body.operationName inside the handler to distinguish queries from mutations
Call req.reply({ data: ... }) to return a stubbed response immediately from inside the handler
Call req.continue() for non-matching operations so they reach the real server unmodified
Define a reusable helper function like interceptGql(name, data) to avoid repeating the same intercept boilerplate

title: The Network Sentinel
story: In complex pages, multiple requests fly at once. The Network Sentinel waits on several network calls simultaneously, inspects the full request and response objects, and asserts network contracts — not just the UI.
objective: Alias multiple intercepts and use cy.wait() on an array of aliases to assert on request headers, response status codes, response bodies, and call counts.
hints: cy.wait(["@alias1", "@alias2"]) returns an array of interception objects in the same order as the aliases
interception.request has .method, .url, .headers, and .body
interception.response has .statusCode, .headers, and .body
Use cy.get("@alias.all") to get an array of every call to that intercept — great for asserting call counts

title: The Promise Alchemist

stub.onFirstCall().resolves(...) and stub.onSecondCall().rejects(...) let you simulate retry and failure sequences

title: The Time Freezer
story: Date.now() lies — its value changes every millisecond, making date-dependent tests flaky. The Time Freezer locks the clock at a precise moment before the page even loads, so every timestamp is predictable and testable.

cy.clock() must be called BEFORE cy.visit() to freeze time during the initial page load
Cypress automatically restores the real clock after each test — call clock.restore() inside the test for early restoration

story: Exact equality is too rigid. The Sinon Matchmaker wields flexible matchers — sinon.match.string, sinon.match.object, sinon.match.has() — to assert that a stub was called with the right shape of argument, not necessarily the exact value.
objective: Use sinon matchers inside calledWith assertions to verify that stubs and spies are called with arguments matching a specific type or shape.
hints: sinon.match.string, sinon.match.number, sinon.match.object, sinon.match.array are type matchers
sinon.match.has(key, value) checks that the argument object has a specific property with that value
