title: The Cross-Origin Courier
story: Some journeys cross domain boundaries. The Cross-Origin Courier masters cy.origin() — the spell that lets you interact with pages on different domains without violating the same-origin policy.
objective: Use cy.origin() to visit and interact with a page on a different origin.
hints: cy.origin(url, () => { }) lets you run Cypress commands in a different origin context
Inside cy.origin(), all cy.* commands run against the new origin
You must pass any variables into cy.origin() via the args option: cy.origin(url, { args: { val } }, ({ val }) => { })

title: The Cross-Origin Courier — passes args into cy.origin
story: Variables from the outer test scope must be explicitly passed into cy.origin() via the args option. The courier learns to carry data across domain boundaries.
objective: Pass variables into cy.origin() using the args option.
hints: cy.origin(url, { args: { myVar } }, ({ myVar }) => { cy.get(myVar) })
args must be serialisable — no functions or class instances
Destructure the args in the callback parameter

title: The Cross-Origin Courier — assertions inside cy.origin
story: All Cypress assertions work inside cy.origin(). The courier verifies text, visibility, and attributes on the foreign page.
objective: Run should() assertions inside a cy.origin() block.
hints: .should() works normally inside cy.origin()
cy.contains() also works inside cy.origin()
cy.url() inside cy.origin() returns the URL of the new origin

title: The Cross-Origin Courier — navigates back after cy.origin
story: After visiting a foreign domain, the courier returns home. cy.go('back') and cy.visit() restore the original origin.
objective: Return to the original origin after a cy.origin() block.
hints: After cy.origin() completes, Cypress is back in the primary origin
cy.visit() after cy.origin() targets the primary origin again
cy.url() outside cy.origin() returns the primary origin URL

title: The Cross-Origin Courier — cookies across origins
story: Cookies do not cross origins by default. The courier uses cy.setCookie() before entering the foreign domain.
objective: Set a cookie then use cy.origin() to verify it on the target origin.
hints: cy.setCookie() before cy.origin() sets the cookie for the primary origin
Pass cookie values via args if you need them inside cy.origin()
cy.getCookie() inside cy.origin() retrieves cookies for that origin

title: The Shell Commander
story: Beyond the browser, the Shell Commander issues orders to the operating system itself. cy.exec() runs shell commands during test execution — seeding databases, clearing caches, running scripts.
objective: Use cy.exec() to run a shell command and inspect its output.
hints: cy.exec('command') runs a shell command and yields { code, stdout, stderr }
Assert on the exit code: .its('code').should('eq', 0)
cy.exec() runs in the project root by default

title: The Shell Commander — checks exit code
story: A command that exits with code 0 succeeded. The Shell Commander always verifies the exit code before trusting the result.
objective: Assert that cy.exec() returns exit code 0.
hints: cy.exec() yields { code, stdout, stderr }
.its('code').should('eq', 0) asserts success
Non-zero exit codes indicate failure — Cypress will fail the test by default unless failOnNonZeroExit: false

title: The Shell Commander — ignores non-zero exit
story: Some commands intentionally exit with a non-zero code. The Shell Commander uses failOnNonZeroExit to suppress the failure when needed.
objective: Run cy.exec() with failOnNonZeroExit: false to allow non-zero exit codes.
hints: cy.exec(cmd, { failOnNonZeroExit: false }) allows non-zero exits
You can still assert on .its('code') to know the actual code
Useful when running lint checks that return 1 when issues are found

title: The Shell Commander — reads stderr output
story: Error output flows through stderr. The Shell Commander reads it just as easily as stdout.
objective: Run cy.exec() and inspect the stderr output.
hints: cy.exec() yields { code, stdout, stderr }
.its('stderr') accesses error output
Both stdout and stderr are strings — use .should('contain', ...)

title: The Shell Commander — runs a Node script
story: Node.js scripts can be executed directly. The Shell Commander uses cy.exec() to run a one-liner Node script and validate its output.
objective: Use cy.exec() to run a Node.js script via the command line.
hints: cy.exec('node -e "console.log(42)"') runs inline Node code
The output appears in stdout
Useful for seeding test data or resetting state

title: The Scroll Reader
story: Ancient knowledge is stored in files. The Scroll Reader uses cy.readFile() to retrieve that knowledge during tests — reading fixtures, configs, and generated outputs.
objective: Use cy.readFile() to read a file and assert on its contents.
hints: cy.readFile('path/to/file') yields the file contents as a string
Add encoding as second arg: cy.readFile('file.txt', 'utf8')
cy.readFile() retries until the file exists — useful after cy.exec()

title: The Scroll Reader — asserts on JSON contents
story: JSON files yield parsed objects. The Scroll Reader drills into nested properties using .its().
objective: Read a JSON file and assert on a nested property.
hints: cy.readFile() auto-parses JSON files into objects
.its('key') accesses a property of the yielded object
Chain .should('eq', value) after .its() to assert the value

title: The Scroll Reader — reads file written by exec
story: First the Shell Commander writes a file, then the Scroll Reader reads it. A classic pattern for passing data between cy.exec() and cy.readFile().
objective: Write a file with cy.exec() then read it back with cy.readFile().
hints: cy.exec('echo "hello" > /tmp/test.txt') writes a file
cy.readFile('/tmp/test.txt') reads it back
cy.readFile() retries automatically — no need for cy.wait()

title: The Scroll Reader — retries until file exists
story: cy.readFile() retries automatically. The Scroll Reader waits patiently for a file to appear — no cy.wait() needed.
objective: Demonstrate cy.readFile() retry behaviour with a timeout option.
hints: cy.readFile(path, { timeout: 10000 }) retries for up to 10 seconds
Combine with cy.exec() that generates the file asynchronously
This avoids fragile cy.wait(N) patterns

title: The Scroll Reader — reads text encoding
story: Binary files and plain text need different encodings. The Scroll Reader specifies the encoding to get the right representation.
objective: Use cy.readFile() with an explicit encoding like utf8 or base64.
hints: cy.readFile(path, 'utf8') returns a plain string
cy.readFile(path, 'base64') returns base64-encoded content
Default encoding is utf8 for text files

title: The Scroll Scribe
story: The Scroll Scribe inscribes test results and data into files using cy.writeFile(). Test outputs become readable records for future reference.
objective: Use cy.writeFile() to write data to a file during a test.
hints: cy.writeFile(path, contents) writes a file
Contents can be a string, object (written as JSON), or Buffer
cy.writeFile() creates parent directories automatically

title: The Scroll Scribe — writes JSON
story: Objects are automatically serialised to JSON. The Scribe stores structured data for later retrieval.
objective: Write a JavaScript object to a file as JSON using cy.writeFile().
hints: cy.writeFile(path, { key: value }) writes prettified JSON
cy.readFile() will auto-parse it back to an object
Useful for storing test-generated IDs for later tests

title: The Scroll Scribe — appends to a file
story: The Scribe can append lines without erasing previous inscriptions. The flag option controls write vs append mode.
objective: Use cy.writeFile() with the flag option to append to an existing file.
hints: cy.writeFile(path, content, { flag: 'a+' }) appends
Default flag is 'w' — overwrites the file
Useful for accumulating log output across multiple tests

title: The Scroll Scribe — writes and re-reads between tests
story: Data written in one test can be read back in another. The Scribe uses beforeEach and cy.readFile() to share state without brittle globals.
objective: Write a file in one test and read it back in a subsequent test.
hints: cy.writeFile in beforeEach is a good pattern for shared test data
Avoid using JavaScript variables across tests — prefer cy.readFile()
cy.writeFile is synchronous from Cypress's perspective — it completes before the next command

title: The Scroll Scribe — overwrites fixture file
story: Test fixtures sometimes need resetting. The Scribe overwrites them cleanly before each run.
objective: Use cy.writeFile() to reset a fixture before a test runs.
hints: cy.writeFile('cypress/fixtures/data.json', { ... }) overwrites the fixture
Do this in beforeEach to ensure a clean state
cy.fixture() will then read the freshly written version

title: The Environment Oracle
story: Test configuration varies by environment. The Environment Oracle reads from Cypress.env() to keep credentials, URLs, and flags out of test code.
objective: Use Cypress.env() to read an environment variable inside a test.
hints: Cypress.env('KEY') reads a variable set in cypress.config.js env block
You can also set env vars via CLI: --env KEY=value
Cypress.env() returns all env vars as an object when called with no arguments

title: The Environment Oracle — reads a specific key
story: Each variable has a name. The Oracle reads a specific key and uses it in the test logic.
objective: Read a specific Cypress env key and use its value.
hints: Cypress.env('KEY') returns the value for that key, or undefined if not set
You can set a default: const val = Cypress.env('KEY') || 'default'
Avoid hardcoding secrets — use Cypress.env() instead

title: The Environment Oracle — sets an env variable at runtime
story: The Oracle can inscribe new variables during the test run. Cypress.env(key, value) sets a variable for the remainder of the spec.
objective: Set a Cypress env variable at runtime and read it back.
hints: Cypress.env('KEY', value) sets the variable for the current spec
Changes do not persist beyond the current spec file
Useful for sharing state between tests without global variables

title: The Environment Oracle — uses env in cy.visit()
story: Base URLs from environment variables keep tests portable. The Oracle constructs the full URL from Cypress.env() before navigating.
objective: Construct a cy.visit() URL using a value from Cypress.env().
hints: Cypress.config('baseUrl') reads the configured base URL
Combine Cypress.env() values to build dynamic paths
This pattern makes tests portable across staging/production

title: The Environment Oracle — Cypress.config()
story: Beyond env vars, the Oracle reads Cypress configuration values at runtime. Cypress.config() exposes timeout, baseUrl, viewportWidth and more.
objective: Use Cypress.config() to read a configuration value at runtime.
hints: Cypress.config('defaultCommandTimeout') returns the default timeout in ms
Cypress.config('viewportWidth') returns current viewport width
Cypress.config('baseUrl') returns the configured base URL

title: The Great Purge
story: Between tests, stale cookies and storage can leak state. The Great Purge uses clearAllCookies, clearAllLocalStorage, and clearAllSessionStorage to wipe the slate clean.
objective: Use cy.clearAllCookies() to remove all cookies.
hints: cy.clearAllCookies() removes all cookies for all domains
Cypress already clears cookies between tests by default
Use explicitly when you need to clear mid-test

title: The Great Purge — clears all localStorage
story: localStorage persists between page loads. The Purge sweeps it away with cy.clearAllLocalStorage().
objective: Use cy.clearAllLocalStorage() to remove all localStorage entries.
hints: cy.clearAllLocalStorage() clears localStorage for all origins
cy.getAllLocalStorage() returns an object of all local storage by origin
Cypress clears localStorage between tests by default

title: The Great Purge — clears all sessionStorage
story: sessionStorage lasts for the tab session. The Purge eliminates it with cy.clearAllSessionStorage().
objective: Use cy.clearAllSessionStorage() to remove all sessionStorage entries.
hints: cy.clearAllSessionStorage() clears sessionStorage for all origins
cy.getAllSessionStorage() returns current sessionStorage contents
sessionStorage is cleared when the tab closes — but Cypress keeps the page open

title: The Great Purge — reads all localStorage with getAllLocalStorage
story: Before purging, the Archivist inventories all stored data using cy.getAllLocalStorage().
objective: Use cy.getAllLocalStorage() to inspect all localStorage values.
hints: cy.getAllLocalStorage() yields { origin: { key: value } }
The result is keyed by origin URL
Useful for assertions before and after a purge

title: The Great Purge — full storage reset in beforeEach
story: The cleanest tests start with a completely empty state. The Purge runs in beforeEach to guarantee isolation.
objective: Clear all cookies, localStorage and sessionStorage in beforeEach.
hints: Chain all three clear commands in beforeEach for total isolation
This pattern prevents test pollution from any source
Cypress default test isolation only handles cookies — do localStorage manually if needed

title: The Annotation Scribe
story: Tests tell stories. The Annotation Scribe uses cy.log() to add readable messages to the Cypress command log — marking key steps without affecting test execution.
objective: Use cy.log() to add a custom message to the Cypress command log.
hints: cy.log('message') adds a blue annotation in the command log
cy.log() does not affect test pass/fail status
Use template literals for dynamic messages: cy.log(`User: ${name}`)

title: The Annotation Scribe — logs variable values
story: Inspecting values mid-test is powerful. The Scribe logs them with template literals.
objective: Use cy.log() to output a dynamic value during the test.
hints: cy.log(`Value: ${someVar}`) logs the current value
cy.log() inside .then() gives you access to the subject
This is more visible than console.log during test runs

title: The Annotation Scribe — groups log messages
story: Complex tests benefit from section markers. The Scribe uses cy.log() to separate phases: setup, action, assertion.
objective: Use cy.log() as section headers to structure a multi-step test.
hints: Use cy.log() before each phase: setup, act, assert
It creates a readable narrative in the Cypress time-travel log
No performance cost — cy.log() is synchronous and instant

title: The Annotation Scribe — logs inside each iteration
story: When iterating with .each(), the Scribe logs each item to track progress through the loop.
objective: Use cy.log() inside a .each() loop to output the current item.
hints: cy.log() inside .each() logs per iteration
Combine with the index parameter to show progress
cy.log() yields null — chain cy.wrap() if you need to continue a chain after it

title: The Annotation Scribe — logs with multiple args
story: cy.log() accepts multiple arguments separated by spaces. The Scribe uses this to log labels alongside values.
objective: Call cy.log() with multiple arguments.
hints: cy.log('label', value) joins both with a space in the log
You can pass objects — they are serialized with JSON.stringify
Unlike console.log, cy.log appears in the Cypress UI timeline

title: The Debug Sentinel
story: When a test fails unexpectedly, the Debug Sentinel halts execution mid-stream. cy.pause() freezes time so you can inspect the DOM manually.
objective: Understand cy.pause() — place it in a test to pause execution interactively.
hints: cy.pause() stops test execution and shows a Resume button in the runner
Only useful in open (interactive) mode — has no effect in headless runs
Remove cy.pause() before committing — it will hang CI

title: The Debug Sentinel — cy.debug() logs the subject
story: .debug() prints the current subject to the browser console. The Sentinel uses it to inspect what a command yields before asserting.
objective: Chain .debug() on a command to log its subject to the console.
hints: .debug() logs the current subject to the console and yields it unchanged
It is a pass-through — chaining after it works normally
Unlike cy.pause(), .debug() does not halt execution

title: The Debug Sentinel — cy.debug() on a value
story: The Sentinel inspects plain values, not just DOM elements. .debug() works anywhere in the chain.
objective: Use cy.debug() on a non-DOM value like a string or number.
hints: cy.wrap(value).debug() logs the wrapped value
.debug() yields the subject unchanged so you can continue asserting
Check the browser console (F12) to see the debug output

title: The Debug Sentinel — uses cy.then for manual inspection
story: When automated debugging is not enough, the Sentinel uses .then() to run arbitrary code — console.log, debugger, or custom logic.
objective: Use .then() as a manual debugging point inside a test.
hints: .then(subject => { console.log(subject) }) lets you inspect anything
The debugger statement inside .then() triggers browser devtools
.then() is synchronous within the Cypress command queue

title: The Debug Sentinel — using Cypress.log for custom events
story: Advanced sentinels create custom log entries with Cypress.log(). This lets plugins and custom commands appear in the timeline.
objective: Create a custom Cypress log entry using Cypress.log().
hints: Cypress.log({ name, message }) creates a custom timeline entry
Useful inside custom commands to make them visible in the runner
Different from cy.log() — this is the low-level API

title: The Browser Oracle
story: Tests run on Chrome, Firefox, Edge — each with subtle differences. The Browser Oracle uses Cypress.isBrowser() and Cypress.browser to adapt behaviour at runtime.
objective: Use Cypress.browser to read the current browser name and version.
hints: Cypress.browser.name returns 'chrome', 'firefox', 'electron', etc.
Cypress.browser.version returns the browser version string
Cypress.browser.isHeadless is true when running headlessly

title: The Browser Oracle — isBrowser() for conditional logic
story: Some features only work in specific browsers. The Oracle uses Cypress.isBrowser() to skip or adjust tests conditionally.
objective: Use Cypress.isBrowser() to conditionally run assertions.
hints: Cypress.isBrowser('chrome') returns true when running in Chrome
Cypress.isBrowser(['chrome', 'edge']) accepts an array
Use this for browser-specific feature tests

title: The Browser Oracle — skips test in specific browser
story: The Oracle instructs the test runner to skip a test when running in an incompatible browser.
objective: Use Cypress.isBrowser() to conditionally skip a test.
hints: Combine Cypress.isBrowser() with it.skip() for conditional skipping
if (Cypress.isBrowser('firefox')) return; inside the test body also works
This prevents false failures from browser-specific quirks

title: The Browser Oracle — reads isHeadless flag
story: CI runs Cypress headlessly. The Oracle checks Cypress.browser.isHeadless to change behaviour in CI vs local.
objective: Read Cypress.browser.isHeadless and use it in a conditional.
hints: Cypress.browser.isHeadless is true in 'cypress run' mode
It is false when running in 'cypress open' mode
Use it to skip slow visual assertions in CI

title: The Browser Oracle — reads browser family
story: Chrome, Chromium, and Edge share the same engine. The Oracle identifies the browser family to handle them uniformly.
objective: Use Cypress.browser.family to detect the browser rendering engine.
hints: Cypress.browser.family is 'chromium' for Chrome, Chromium, Edge
Cypress.browser.family is 'firefox' for Firefox
Cypress.browser.family is 'webkit' for WebKit-based browsers

title: The File Chooser
story: The File Chooser wields .selectFile() — the modern Cypress API for simulating file selection in <input type="file"> elements, replacing the old workarounds.
objective: Use .selectFile() to attach a file to an input element.
hints: .selectFile('cypress/fixtures/example.json') attaches a real fixture file
.selectFile() targets <input type="file"> elements
Cypress resolves the file path relative to the project root

title: The File Chooser — selects a virtual file
story: No file needed on disk. The Chooser creates a virtual file in memory using the contents option.
objective: Use .selectFile() with a virtual file defined by contents.
hints: .selectFile({ contents: 'data', fileName: 'test.txt' }) creates a virtual file
contents can be a string, Cypress.Buffer, or Blob
Useful when you want to test without fixture files on disk

title: The File Chooser — selects multiple files
story: Multi-file inputs need an array. The Chooser passes multiple files in one call.
objective: Use .selectFile() with an array to select multiple files.
hints: .selectFile([file1, file2]) selects multiple files
The input must have the multiple attribute
Each item can be a path string or a virtual file object

title: The File Chooser — drag and drop with selectFile
story: Some upload zones accept drag-and-drop. The Chooser uses the drag-drop action option to simulate this.
objective: Use .selectFile() with action: 'drag-drop' to simulate dropping a file.
hints: .selectFile(file, { action: 'drag-drop' }) triggers dragover and drop events
The target element must have drag event listeners
Useful for upload zones that do not use <input type="file">

title: The File Chooser — reads input files after selection
story: After selecting, the Chooser verifies the file was received by reading the input's files property.
objective: Assert on the files property of an input after .selectFile().
hints: After .selectFile(), use .then(input => input[0].files) to access the FileList
.its('files.length') asserts how many files are attached
The files property is a native FileList object

title: The Shadow Realm
story: Web components hide their internals in a Shadow DOM — invisible to normal selectors. The Shadow Realm wizard pierces through using .shadow() to reach the hidden elements.
objective: Use .shadow() to access elements inside a Shadow DOM.
hints: .shadow() pierces the shadow boundary of a host element
cy.get('my-component').shadow().find('button') queries inside the shadow root
Alternatively, enable experimentalShadowDomSupport in cypress.config.js

title: The Shadow Realm — finds nested shadow elements
story: Elements inside the shadow tree are found with .find() after crossing the shadow boundary.
objective: Chain .find() after .shadow() to locate a nested element.
hints:
cy.get('host').shadow().find('p') finds a

inside the shadow root
.find() works on shadow roots the same as on regular DOM trees
Nested shadow roots require chaining .shadow() multiple times

title: The Shadow Realm — clicks inside shadow DOM
story: Interactions inside shadow DOM work the same as in the regular DOM after crossing the boundary.
objective: Click an element inside a Shadow DOM using .shadow().find().click().
hints: cy.get('host').shadow().find('button').click() triggers events inside shadow DOM
Event propagation crosses shadow boundaries for most standard events
Shadow DOM clicks are subject to the same actionability checks

title: The Shadow Realm — includeShadowDom option
story: Enable includeShadowDom globally to make cy.get() pierce all shadow roots automatically.
objective: Use the includeShadowDom option to pierce shadow DOM without calling .shadow().
hints: cy.get('selector', { includeShadowDom: true }) pierces shadow roots globally
Set Cypress.config('includeShadowDom', true) to apply globally for a spec
This is useful when working with deeply nested web components

title: The Shadow Realm — asserts text inside shadow DOM
story: Text content inside shadow DOM is accessible with .should('have.text') after crossing the shadow boundary.
objective: Assert text content of an element inside Shadow DOM.
hints: .shadow().find('p').should('have.text', '...') asserts shadow element text
.shadow().find('p').invoke('text') extracts the text as a string
Chai text assertions work identically on shadow elements

title: The Focus Detective
story: Keyboard navigation and accessibility depend on focus management. The Focus Detective uses cy.focused() to get the currently focused element and assert it is the right one.
objective: Use cy.focused() to get the currently focused element.
hints: cy.focused() yields the element that currently has focus
If no element is focused, cy.focused() fails — use cy.focused({ log: false }) to suppress the error
Chain should() on cy.focused() to assert on the focused element

title: The Focus Detective — asserts focused element type
story: The Detective checks not just which element is focused, but what kind of element it is.
objective: Assert the tag name of the focused element using cy.focused().
hints: cy.focused().invoke('prop', 'tagName') returns the tag name in uppercase
cy.focused().should('have.prop', 'tagName', 'INPUT') asserts the tag
Or: cy.focused().should('match', 'input') using CSS selector matching

title: The Focus Detective — tab key moves focus
story: The Tab key moves focus between interactive elements. The Detective verifies focus moves correctly after pressing Tab.
objective: Press Tab and use cy.focused() to verify focus moved to the next element.
hints: cy.focused().type('{tab}') or cy.get(el).type('{tab}') moves focus
After tabbing, cy.focused() yields the newly focused element
Test accessibility of keyboard navigation this way

title: The Focus Detective — blur removes focus
story: Calling .blur() removes focus from an element. The Detective verifies focus is no longer on the element after blurring.
objective: Use .blur() and verify cy.focused() no longer returns the blurred element.
hints: .blur() removes focus from the currently focused element
After blur, cy.focused() may return a different element or fail
Blur events trigger validation in many form libraries

title: The Focus Detective — have.focus assertion
story: The simplest focus assertion. The Detective uses .should('have.focus') directly on an element.
objective: Assert that a specific element has focus using should('have.focus').
hints: .should('have.focus') asserts the element is currently focused
.should('not.have.focus') asserts it is not focused
This is equivalent to document.activeElement === el

title: The Array Spreader
story: When a command yields an array, .spread() distributes each item as a separate argument to a callback. The Spreader handles multi-value yields with elegance.
objective: Use .spread() to destructure an array yielded by a Cypress command.
hints: .spread(fn) calls fn with each array item as a separate argument
Like .then() but spreads the array: .spread((a, b) => { })
Works on any command that yields an array

title: The Array Spreader — spreads cookie array
story: cy.getCookies() yields an array of cookies. The Spreader extracts each one by position.
objective: Use .spread() on cy.getCookies() to access individual cookies.
hints: cy.setCookie() then cy.getCookies() then .spread((c1) => { }) works
Each spread argument is a cookie object with name, value, domain, etc.
.spread() is preferable to .then((cookies) => cookies[0]) for clarity

title: The Array Spreader — spreads Promise.all results
story: Resolving multiple promises at once yields an array. The Spreader unpacks each resolved value.
objective: Use .spread() after resolving multiple Cypress.Promise values.
hints: cy.wrap(Promise.all([p1, p2])).spread((r1, r2) => { })
Each argument corresponds to a resolved promise
Useful when fetching multiple resources in parallel

title: The Array Spreader — spreads multiple elements
story: After getting multiple elements, the Spreader accesses each by position in the callback.
objective: Use .spread() on a multi-element result to access individual elements.
hints: cy.get('li').then($els => [...$els]).spread((el1, el2) => { }) spreads DOM elements
Convert jQuery collection to array first with [...$els]
Useful for comparing two specific elements side by side

title: The Array Spreader — spreads aliases
story: Multiple aliases can be collected into an array and spread. The Spreader accesses each aliased subject by name in the callback.
objective: Collect multiple aliases and spread them in a then callback.
hints: Store values using .as('name'), then retrieve with cy.get('@name')
To spread, collect all aliases first into an array
cy.get('@a') and cy.get('@b') return separate subjects — wrap them in an array

title: The Root Seeker
story: Every DOM tree has a root. The Root Seeker uses cy.root() to get the document root element, and .root() to get the root within a .within() scope.
objective: Use cy.root() to get the document root element.
hints: cy.root() yields the <html> element by default
Inside cy.within(), cy.root() yields the scoped element instead
Useful for resetting scope after deep traversals

title: The Root Seeker — root inside within()
story: Inside a .within() block, cy.root() returns the scoped element, not the document root. The Seeker uses this to escape the scope when needed.
objective: Call cy.root() inside a .within() block and see it returns the scoped element.
hints: Inside .within($el => { cy.root() }), cy.root() returns $el
This lets you get a reference to the within scope
It is the equivalent of "return to the top of this scope"

title: The Root Seeker — chains from root
story: Starting from the root ensures the selector is not accidentally scoped. The Seeker chains cy.root().find() to perform an absolute DOM query.
objective: Chain .find() from cy.root() to perform an absolute query.
hints: cy.root().find('selector') queries from the document root
This overrides any active .within() scope
Useful to break out of a scope without ending the within block

title: The Root Seeker — root vs document()
story: The Seeker compares cy.root() with cy.document() — both give access to the page top, but via different yields.
objective: Compare cy.root() and cy.document() to understand what each yields.
hints: cy.root() yields the <html> DOM element
cy.document() yields the document object (not a DOM element)
cy.document().its('documentElement') equals cy.root()

title: The Root Seeker — resets scope with root
story: Deep within a complex DOM, the Seeker resets to root to start fresh without ending the within block.
objective: Use cy.root() to reset context after navigating deep into the DOM.
hints: cy.root() inside .within() returns the scoped container, not the document
Outside .within(), cy.root() always yields <html>
Use cy.root().find() to restart a query from the top of scope
